lesson.title: Real Plus Imaginary: Adding Impedances in Rectangular Form
lesson.summary: Rectangular form writes a complex number as a real part plus an imaginary part, the natural format for adding or subtracting the impedances and phasors that show up constantly in AC circuit analysis.
lesson.body:
Rectangular form writes a complex number as z = a + jb, where a is the real part, b is the imaginary part, and j = sqrt(-1) is used instead of the mathematician's i to avoid clashing with the symbol for current. In circuit analysis this format shows up constantly because impedance itself is a complex number: Z = R + jX, where the real part R is resistance and the imaginary part X is reactance, positive for inductive reactance and negative for capacitive reactance.

The whole reason rectangular form earns a name and a chapter of its own is that it is the natural format for addition and subtraction. To add two complex numbers in rectangular form, you simply add the real parts together and add the imaginary parts together, exactly the way you would add two vectors given in x and y components. That matters directly for circuits, because impedances in series add exactly this way, Z_total = Z1 + Z2, and admittances in parallel add the same way, so any calculation involving series combinations essentially requires converting to, or already having, rectangular form.

Consider two impedances connected in series, Z1 = 3 + j4 ohms and Z2 = 2 - j1 ohms. To find the total series impedance, add the real parts and the imaginary parts separately: the real part is 3 + 2 = 5, and the imaginary part is 4 + (-1) = 3. So Z_total = Z1 + Z2 = 5 + j3 ohms. Notice this addition took two lines of simple arithmetic, no trigonometry required, which is exactly the convenience rectangular form provides.

Subtraction works the same way, just with a sign flip: Z1 - Z2 = (3 - 2) + j(4 - (-1)) = 1 + j5 ohms. This kind of subtraction shows up whenever Kirchhoff's voltage law is applied around a phasor loop, since a loop equation typically asks for the difference between two complex voltage or impedance terms, not just their sum, and rectangular form handles that subtraction with the same term by term simplicity as addition.

Rectangular form does have a real weakness: multiplication and division of two numbers in the a + jb format require the full complex multiplication rule, (a + jb)(c + jd) = (ac - bd) + j(ad + bc), which is more work than it needs to be. Because Ohm's law in phasor form, V = IZ, is a multiplication, rectangular form is rarely the most convenient format for that particular step, and the next chapter's polar form exists specifically to make multiplication and division simple instead.

From the result above, Z_total = 5 + j3 ohms, it is still possible to extract the magnitude and angle directly, using the same right triangle relationships used for any complex number: magnitude |Z| = sqrt(5^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(25 + 9) = sqrt(34), about 5.83 ohms, and angle theta = arctan(3/5), about 30.96 degrees. Keeping both representations, rectangular for adding and polar for multiplying, on hand at the same time is the standard working style for anyone doing AC circuit analysis by hand.
